description: Hi! I am a high school student passionate about astrophysics, space exploration, solar system, planets and stars. Ready to create inspiring and creative space project!
summary: SPHEREx Time-Shift Explorer is a browser-based tool concept designed to make NASA’s multi-epoch SPHEREx infrared sky surveys accessible without downloading heavy FITS files or using complex software. To address the challenge of finding faint moving and variable objects across billions of infrared frames, my tool aligns 6-month survey images onto a single coordinate grid, subtracts stationary background stars, and lets users blink between epochs across 102 spectral bands (0.75 to 5.0 µm). This approach is important because it removes technical barriers for students, citizen scientists, and researchers, allowing them to spot fast-moving brown dwarfs, variable stars, and slow-moving Planet X candidates in seconds. I demonstrated this concept using official catalog data and archival sky images for Barnard’s Star, WISE 0855, and R Draconis.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

SPHEREx Time-Shift Explorer is a browser-based tool concept that displays multi-epoch infrared images from NASA’s SPHEREx mission so anyone can see how space objects change over time. Users simply enter sky coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination) or an object name to load cutouts from the SPHEREx archive. The tool automatically aligns sequential 6-month survey frames onto one coordinate grid, keeping stationary background stars in place. Users can then rapidly flip between dates in blink mode or use difference imaging to subtract static background stars, making moving objects jump out right away. They can also switch across SPHEREx’s 102 near-infrared bands (0.75 to 5.0 µm) to spot cold brown dwarfs and track brightness changes in variable stars.

Benefits & Intended Impact

SPHEREx scans the entire sky every six months across 102 infrared bands, creating too much data for scientists to check manually. At the same time, downloading and analyzing massive FITS files requires strong computers and special software. My tool removes this barrier and opens the SPHEREx archive to students, citizen scientists, and researchers right in a standard web browser. It speeds up the search for fast-moving neighbors, pulsating stars, and slow-moving outer Solar System candidates like Planet X.

Creativity & Demonstration

To show how the tool works in practice, I demonstrated the concept on real astronomical targets listed in the NASA challenge. Using official catalog data and archival sky images from NASA/IPAC IRSA, ESA Gaia DR3, and WiseView, I showed how fast-moving neighbors like Barnard’s Star and the brown dwarf WISE 0855 shift position across 6-month survey cycles, how infrared cutouts reveal brightness changes in the variable star R Draconis, and how background star subtraction can help isolate a slow-moving Planet X candidate.


Tools & Resources Used

To build and present this project, I worked with NASA/IPAC IRSA archives, SPHEREx mission specifications and Quick Release documentation, ESA Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020 catalogs, WiseView for checking multi-epoch sky images and background subtraction, and Overleaf (LaTeX) to format the final report.

Factors Considered

While developing this project, I focused on three key practical factors:

- Survey Timing & Speed: Different objects move at very different speeds across 6-month survey cycles (from fast nearby brown dwarfs to a very slow Planet X), so the tool needs both rapid blinking and background star subtraction.

- Structure Before Design: During the hackathon, I learned that building a solid content structure first is much more effective than starting with visual decoration. I prioritized organizing the project logic, verifying official NASA and partner resources, and then formatting the final document in Overleaf.

- Accessibility: Every feature was designed so that a beginner with no special software can explore real space telescope data in seconds.
